module_title: Module 8 Lesson 1: Sizing and Installing Water Storage

lessons.title: Module 8 Lesson 1: Sizing and Installing Water Storage Tanks for African Homes and Businesses
lessons.body: Water storage is not a luxury in most African plumbing projects; it is the backbone of reliability. Whether you are working in Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, Kampala, or a rural growth centre, the municipal supply is often intermittent, pressure is low, and power cuts interrupt pumping. A well-sized and properly installed storage tank keeps taps running, protects pumps, and creates business opportunities for plumbers who understand design, hygiene, and maintenance. This lesson covers practical tank sizing, siting, installation, and the commercial angle. Start with demand. A typical household in urban Africa uses between 100 and 200 litres per person per day when water is available. In a home with six people, that is 600 to 1,200 litres daily. If the supply comes only three days a week, you need storage for at least three days plus a reserve. A simple formula is daily demand multiplied by days of autonomy, then add 20 percent for future growth and cleaning losses. For a six-person home with three-day autonomy, 1,200 litres per day times three days equals 3,600 litres, plus 20 percent gives about 4,320 litres. In practice, you would specify two 2,500-litre tanks or one 5,000-litre tank. For small businesses, calculate differently. A guesthouse with 20 rooms may use 4,000 to 6,000 litres per day. A restaurant may use 2,000 to 3,000 litres per day. A school with 300 pupils may use 3,000 to 5,000 litres per day. Always ask the client about peak days, visitors, laundry, irrigation, and cleaning. Tank material matters. Polyethylene tanks are popular because they are affordable, lightweight, and resistant to corrosion. They come in sizes from 100 litres to 20,000 litres. They must be food-grade and UV-stabilised if installed outdoors. Concrete tanks are durable and can be built on site, but they need proper curing, waterproofing, and cleaning access. Steel tanks are strong but require anti-rust treatment and are less common for potable water. Galvanised tanks can leach zinc and should not be used for drinking water unless lined. In coastal areas, salt air corrodes metal quickly, so plastic or concrete is better. Siting is critical. Place tanks on a stable, level base, preferably a reinforced concrete slab at least 100 mm thick with a compacted hardcore sub-base. The base must extend at least 150 mm beyond the tank footprint. Never place a tank directly on bare ground, because soil movement, termites, and moisture can damage it. Keep tanks away from septic tanks, soak pits, and livestock areas by at least 15 metres if possible, and never downhill from a latrine. In flood-prone areas, raise the tank on a plinth at least 300 mm above the highest known flood level. In hot climates, shade the tank or use a reflective cover to reduce algae growth and evaporation. Installation follows a sequence. First, confirm the tank is clean and food-grade. Second, install a screened inlet to keep out mosquitoes, leaves, and rodents. Third, fit an overflow pipe that discharges to a safe drainage point away from the foundation. Fourth, install a washout or drain valve at the lowest point for cleaning. Fifth, connect the outlet to the pump or gravity system. If the tank feeds by gravity, the outlet should be at least 150 mm above the tank floor to avoid drawing sediment. If a pump draws from the tank, use a floating suction or a suction line with a foot valve and strainer. Always install a non-return valve to prevent backflow contamination. For pressurised systems, include a pressure tank and pressure switch. For gravity systems, calculate head. A tank 10 metres above the tap gives roughly 1 bar of pressure, which is enough for most domestic fixtures. A tank 5 metres above gives about 0.5 bar, which may be too low for showers and washing machines. In many African homes, tanks are placed on a roof or a steel tower. Roof placement adds structural load, so check the roof design. A 1,000-litre tank weighs one tonne when full, plus the tank itself. That is a serious load. Steel towers must be designed by an engineer, with cross-bracing, concrete footings, and corrosion protection. Water quality is non-negotiable. Tanks must be cleaned every six to twelve months. Sediment, biofilm, and insects accumulate. Train clients to isolate the tank, drain it, scrub the walls with a soft brush and a mild chlorine solution, rinse, and refill. Use 50 mg of granular calcium hypochlorite per litre of tank capacity for disinfection, or follow local health guidelines. Never mix chlorine with other chemicals. Test residual chlorine with a simple test kit. Keep a logbook of cleaning dates, chlorine doses, and water tests. This logbook becomes a selling point for your business. Business-first thinking: do not just sell tanks. Sell a water security package. That includes a site survey, demand calculation, tank supply, base construction, inlet and outlet plumbing, pump selection, first flush diverter, filtration, and a maintenance contract. Price the package, not just the tank. A plumber who installs a 5,000-litre tank and leaves the client to figure out the pump and filter is leaving money on the table. Offer annual cleaning and inspection for a fee. In many cities, landlords and hotels will pay monthly for guaranteed water. That recurring revenue is more valuable than one-off installations. Common mistakes to avoid: undersizing the tank, placing it on weak ground, using non-food-grade containers, forgetting the overflow, burying the tank without access, and connecting rainwater directly to the tank without a first flush diverter. Rainwater harvesting is a big opportunity in Africa. A 100 square metre roof in a region with 800 mm annual rainfall can collect about 80,000 litres per year. That is enough to supply a household for months. But the first rain washes bird droppings, dust, and leaves into the tank. A first flush diverter, a simple pipe that fills and then diverts, keeps the tank cleaner. Also install a leaf screen and a calm inlet to reduce turbulence. Finally, document everything. Take photos of the base, the inlet, the overflow, the outlet, and the label. Give the client a simple manual in English and the local language if possible. Show them how to check for leaks, how to clean the screen, and how to isolate the tank. A client who understands the system will maintain it, recommend you, and call you for the next job. That is how a plumbing business grows in Africa: not by selling parts, but by selling reliable water.

lessons.title: Module 8 Lesson 2: Pump Selection, Installation, and Maintenance for African Water Systems
lessons.body: Pumps are the heart of most pressurised water systems in Africa. They move water from tanks, boreholes, wells, rivers, and dams to homes, farms, and businesses. A wrong pump wastes money, burns electricity, and fails early. A right pump delivers steady pressure for years. This lesson teaches you how to select, install, and maintain pumps in African conditions, where voltage fluctuates, water is often sandy, and maintenance budgets are tight. Start with the basics. Pumps are rated by flow rate, usually in litres per minute or cubic metres per hour, and by head, usually in metres. Head is not just the vertical height. It includes vertical lift, friction losses in pipes and fittings, and pressure required at the outlet. A simple formula is total head equals static lift plus friction loss plus pressure head. Static lift is the vertical distance from the water level to the highest outlet. Friction loss depends on pipe length, diameter, and flow. As a rule of thumb, add 10 to 20 percent of the pipe length for friction in small systems, but for long runs, use friction tables. Pressure head is the pressure you want at the tap. One bar equals about 10 metres of head. If you want 1.5 bar at the shower, that is 15 metres of head. Suppose a tank is 5 metres below the shower, the pipe run is 30 metres, and you want 1.5 bar. Static lift is 5 metres. Friction loss might be 4 metres. Pressure head is 15 metres. Total head is 24 metres. Now choose a pump that delivers the required flow at 24 metres head. Do not choose a pump that only matches the flow at zero head. That is a common mistake. Pump types. Centrifugal pumps are common for clean water and moderate heads. They are simple and affordable. Self-priming pumps can lift water from a few metres below and are good for tanks and shallow wells. Submersible pumps go inside boreholes and wells. They are efficient and quiet but require proper sizing and protection. Jet pumps are used for shallow wells and can self-prime. Diaphragm pumps are good for low flow and dirty water. Solar pumps are increasingly popular in rural Africa because they avoid fuel and grid dependence. For boreholes, you need a submersible pump with a diameter smaller than the borehole casing. A 4-inch borehole typically takes a 3-inch pump. The pump must be set below the water level but above the bottom of the borehole. Install a safety rope, a non-return valve, and a torque arrestor. Use a control box with overload protection and dry-run protection. Dry running destroys pumps. In Africa, dry running happens when the tank empties, the borehole yield drops, or the suction pipe leaks. Install a float switch in the tank and a dry-run sensor on the pump. For solar pumps, size the array carefully. A pump that needs 1,000 watts may need 1,500 watts of panels to account for clouds, dust, and heat. Use a maximum power point tracking controller. In dusty areas, clean panels weekly. In areas with theft risk, mount panels on a secure roof or a fenced structure. Installation best practices. Use a suction line that is short, straight, and at least one size larger than the pump inlet. Use a foot valve with a strainer. Prime the pump before starting. Check rotation direction for three-phase motors. Use correct cable sizes to avoid voltage drop. A 10 percent voltage drop can overheat a motor. In areas with unstable voltage, install a surge protector and an automatic voltage regulator. For generators, ensure the generator is sized for the pump starting current, which can be three to five times the running current. For pressure systems, install a pressure tank. The pressure tank reduces pump cycling, which extends motor life. Set the pressure switch to cut in at 1.5 bar and cut out at 3 bar for domestic systems, or as required. Pre-charge the pressure tank to 0.2 bar below the cut-in pressure. Check the pre-charge annually. Maintenance. Pumps need routine care. Check for leaks, unusual noise, vibration, and overheating. Clean strainers and foot valves. Check the pressure tank pre-charge. Test the dry-run protection. For submersible pumps, check the control box, the cable insulation, and the earthing. In sandy water, install a sediment filter before the pump or use a sand-tolerant pump. In hard water areas, descale with a mild acid solution according to the manufacturer. Keep a maintenance log. In many African contexts, the biggest pump killer is not wear but power quality. Voltage spikes from lightning, grid switching, and generator changeover damage windings. Install lightning arrestors on the power line and earth the pump properly. Use a dedicated circuit. Do not share a pump circuit with welding machines or large motors. Business opportunities. Pumps are a service business. Offer pump selection, installation, commissioning, and maintenance contracts. Many farmers, hotels, and landlords need quarterly pump checks. Charge for call-outs, parts, and labour. Stock common spares: seals, bearings, capacitors, pressure switches, float switches, and foot valves. Train a technician to do pump repairs. In rural areas, solar pump installation and maintenance is a growing market. Governments and NGOs often fund solar water projects, and they need local technicians. Register your business and bid for those contracts. Common mistakes. Oversizing the pump causes high pressure, pipe bursts, and wasted energy. Undersizing causes poor flow and pump overheating. Wrong pipe size causes high friction and low pressure. No non-return valve causes backflow and pump cycling. No dry-run protection causes burned motors. Poor earthing causes electric shock and pump failure. Ignoring voltage causes repeated burnouts. Not priming a self-priming pump causes seal damage. Using the wrong cable size causes voltage drop and overheating. Safety. Pumps use electricity and water, a dangerous combination. Always isolate power before working on a pump. Use residual current devices. Earth all metal parts. Do not work alone on borehole pumps. Use a tripod and a winch to lift submersible pumps safely. Never lower a pump by its cable. Use the safety rope. In summary, pump work is technical but highly rewarding. Master head calculations, pump curves, and electrical protection. Install with care. Maintain with discipline. Document everything. That is how you become the go-to pump expert in your area, and how you build a plumbing business that earns repeat income.

lessons.title: Module 8 Lesson 3: Pipe Materials, Jointing, and Pressure Testing in African Plumbing
lessons.body: Pipes are the veins of a plumbing system. In Africa, the choice of pipe material and the quality of joints determine whether a system lasts five years or fifty. This lesson covers common pipe materials, jointing methods, pressure testing, and the business discipline of doing it right the first time. Common materials. PVC, uPVC, and CPVC are common for cold water and drainage. uPVC is rigid and good for buried mains and drainage. CPVC handles hot water up to about 90 degrees Celsius. PPR, also called polypropylene random copolymer, is popular for hot and cold water in East Africa and increasingly across the continent. It is joined by heat fusion, which creates a strong, leak-free joint. PEX is flexible and good for retrofits and underfloor heating, but it needs special fittings and is less common in some markets. Galvanised steel is still found in older buildings. It is strong but corrodes, scales, and is difficult to repair. Copper is excellent for hot water and potable water but expensive and prone to theft in some areas. HDPE is flexible, tough, and good for buried water lines, borehole risers, and rural water schemes. It is joined by compression fittings or butt fusion. ABS is used for drainage in some countries. Each material has a pressure rating. uPVC class 6 is about 6 bar, class 10 is about 10 bar, and class 16 is about 16 bar. PPR comes in PN10, PN16, PN20, and PN25. HDPE comes in PE63, PE80, and PE100, with pressure ratings from 6 to 16 bar. Always check the marking on the pipe. Do not use drainage pipe for pressure lines. Do not use cold water pipe for hot water. Jointing methods. For uPVC, use solvent cement. Cut the pipe square, deburr, clean with primer, apply cement to both surfaces, insert with a quarter turn, and hold for 30 seconds. Allow 24 hours before pressure testing. For PPR, use a heat fusion tool. Heat the pipe and fitting to the correct temperature, usually 260 degrees Celsius, insert, and hold without twisting. The joint cools in seconds. For HDPE, use compression fittings for small diameters or butt fusion for large diameters. Butt fusion requires a machine, a clean environment, and trained operators. For galvanised steel, use threaded joints with PTFE tape or pipe dope. For copper, use soldered or press fittings. In Africa, where power can be unreliable, choose jointing methods that suit the site. Solvent cement works without power. PPR needs power for the fusion tool, but many sites have a small generator. HDPE butt fusion needs a machine and a clean area. Plan ahead. Pressure testing. Every pressure line must be tested before it is covered or put into service. The test pressure should be 1.5 times the working pressure, or as specified by the engineer. For a 10 bar system, test at 15 bar. For a 6 bar system, test at 9 bar. Fill the line slowly, bleed air, and pressurise. Hold for at least one hour. A drop in pressure indicates a leak. Mark the leak, repair it, and retest. Do not test with air unless the manufacturer allows it, because air testing stores energy and can be dangerous. For drainage lines, test with water or smoke. Fill the line with water and check for leaks at joints. For buried lines, test before backfilling. Take photos of the test gauge and the line. Record the pressure, time, and result. This record protects you if the client later blames you for a leak. Trenching and bedding. Bury pipes below the frost line if frost is a factor, but in most of Africa, frost is not an issue. Bury below the level of vehicle traffic, usually 600 to 900 mm. Use a sand or fine soil bedding of 100 mm below and 150 mm above the pipe. Remove sharp stones. Compact in layers. Install warning tape above the pipe. For HDPE, allow for thermal expansion and contraction by snaking the pipe slightly. For PVC, use expansion joints on long runs. Thrust blocks. At bends, tees, and end caps, water pressure creates thrust. In large diameter pipes, this thrust can push joints apart. Install concrete thrust blocks at these points. The block bears against undisturbed soil. Size the block according to pipe diameter and pressure. A common rule is one cubic metre of concrete per 100 mm of pipe diameter for high pressure, but always follow engineering design. Valves and fittings. Install isolation valves so sections can be repaired without shutting down the whole system. Use gate valves for isolation and globe or ball valves for flow control. Install air release valves at high points and drain valves at low points. Use strainers before pumps and pressure reducers where pressure is high. In Africa, water can be sandy, so strainers and filters are essential. Water hammer. When a valve closes quickly, pressure surges can burst pipes. Install water hammer arrestors, slow-closing valves, or surge tanks. In tall buildings, install pressure reducing valves on lower floors. In pumped systems, install a pressure tank and a soft-start controller. Business discipline. Price your work by the job, not by the hour, but calculate your costs carefully. Include pipe, fittings, cement, labour, transport, testing, and a contingency of 10 to 15 percent. Do not cut corners on pipe class or jointing. A leak call-back costs more than the extra material. Train your team on one jointing method at a time. Certify them if possible. Keep a stock of common fittings: elbows, tees, couplers, reducers, valves, and adaptors. Use a pipe cutter, not a hacksaw, for clean cuts. Deburr every cut. Clean every joint. Use the right cement for the right pipe. Do not mix PVC cement with CPVC unless rated. Do not use too much cement, because it can soften the pipe. Do not assemble in the rain or in dusty conditions. Common mistakes. Mixing pipe materials without adaptors. Using drainage fittings on pressure lines. Not allowing for expansion. Not installing thrust blocks. Not pressure testing. Backfilling before testing. Using the wrong cement. Overtightening threaded joints and cracking them. Not supporting horizontal runs. Not sloping drainage lines correctly. Not installing cleanouts. In Africa, theft of copper and brass is a real risk. Use plastic where possible. Secure outdoor fittings. Mark buried lines with tape and drawings. Give the client as-built drawings. That is professional, and it helps future repairs. In summary, pipes are simple but unforgiving. Choose the right material, joint it correctly, test it properly, and document it. That discipline builds a reputation that wins bigger contracts, from schools and clinics to hotels and factories.

lessons.title: Module 8 Lesson 4: Drainage, Sewerage, and Sanitation Systems for African Conditions
lessons.body: Drainage and sanitation are where plumbing meets public health. In Africa, poor drainage causes flooding, disease, and structural damage. Good drainage protects buildings, roads, and communities. This lesson covers foul water drainage, stormwater drainage, septic systems, and the business of sanitation services. Foul water drainage. Foul water comes from toilets, sinks, showers, and kitchens. It must go to a sewer, a septic tank, or a treatment system. Never discharge foul water into a storm drain or a river. In many African cities, sewer networks are limited, so on-site systems are common. Design rules. Drainage relies on gravity. Pipe must slope continuously. A common slope for 100 mm pipe is 1 in 60, or about 17 mm per metre. For 150 mm pipe, 1 in 100, or 10 mm per metre. For long runs, use the minimum slope that maintains self-cleansing velocity, about 0.6 to 0.75 metres per second. Too little slope causes solids to settle. Too much slope causes water to run away from solids, leaving them behind. Use the right pipe. uPVC drainage pipe is common. It comes in 50, 75, 110, 160, and 200 mm diameters. Use 110 mm for toilets and 50 mm for basins and showers. Use 75 mm for kitchen sinks. Install inspection chambers or rodding eyes at every change of direction, at every junction, and every 15 metres on straight runs. Use a bottle gully with a trap for sinks and showers. Use a floor drain with a trap in wet rooms. Ventilation. Every drainage system needs ventilation to prevent trap siphonage and sewer gas. Install a vent pipe that goes above the roof. The vent should be at least 100 mm above the roof and away from windows. In tall buildings, install a stack vent. In areas with no sewer, install an air admittance valve if allowed, but a true vent is better. Septic tanks. A septic tank is a watertight chamber that separates solids and liquids. The liquid flows to a soakaway or drain field. Size the tank by daily flow and retention time. A common rule is 1,000 litres for a two-bedroom house, 2,000 litres for a four-bedroom house, and 3,000 litres for a six-bedroom house. For schools and clinics, calculate by users. A septic tank should have two compartments. The first compartment holds 60 percent of the volume, the second 40 percent. The inlet and outlet should have tees or baffles to prevent scum from leaving. The outlet should be 50 mm below the inlet. The tank should be vented. It should be emptied every two to five years by a vacuum tanker. In many African cities, there are private desludging services. Partner with them or start your own. Soakaway and drain field. The liquid from the septic tank goes to a soakaway, which is a pit filled with stones, or a drain field, which is a network of perforated pipes in trenches. Size the soakaway by soil percolation. Do a percolation test: dig a hole, fill with water, and measure how fast it drains. Sandy soil drains fast, clay drains slowly. In clay, use a larger area or a raised bed. Keep soakaways at least 15 metres from any water source, 3 metres from a building, and 1 metre from a boundary. Never build a soakaway uphill of a well. Stormwater drainage. Stormwater is rainwater. It must be managed to prevent flooding and erosion. Use gutters, downpipes, channels, culverts, and retention ponds. In cities, blocked drains cause flash floods. Design for the local rainfall intensity. In many African cities, rainfall can be 50 to 100 mm per hour. Size gutters and downpipes accordingly. A 100 square metre roof needs a downpipe of at least 75 mm, and often 110 mm. Use leaf guards. Keep gutters clean. In rural areas, use swales and check dams to slow water and recharge groundwater. Sanitation options. Not every area has sewers. Options include septic tanks, VIP latrines, pour-flush toilets, composting toilets, and biogas systems. Each has a place. VIP latrines are low-cost and good for rural areas. Pour-flush toilets use a small amount of water and can connect to a septic tank or a biogas digester. Biogas systems produce gas for cooking and a nutrient-rich slurry. They need consistent feeding and maintenance. In schools, a block of VIP latrines with handwashing stations is a common and effective solution. Business opportunities. Sanitation is a growing market. Offer septic tank construction, desludging, drain cleaning, and inspection. Buy or hire a vacuum tanker and provide scheduled emptying. Offer drain cleaning with high-pressure jets and cameras. Offer grease trap cleaning for restaurants. Offer stormwater drain maintenance for municipalities and estates. These are recurring services with steady income. In many African countries, governments and NGOs fund sanitation projects. Register your business, get the required permits, and bid for those contracts. Health and safety. Sewage contains pathogens. Wear gloves, boots, and eye protection. Use disinfectant. Wash hands with soap. Do not eat or smoke while working. Vaccinate against hepatitis A and B and tetanus. Use confined space procedures for deep chambers. Test for gas before entering. Never enter a septic tank without breathing apparatus and a standby person. Common mistakes. Not enough slope. Too much slope. No vents. No inspection chambers. Undersized septic tanks. Soakaways too close to wells. Stormwater connected to foul sewers. Foul water connected to storm drains. No grease traps. No cleanouts. Poor workmanship at joints. In Africa, the biggest drainage problem is often maintenance, not design. Train clients to keep drains clear. Provide a maintenance schedule. Offer annual inspections. A well-maintained system lasts decades. A neglected system fails in months. In summary, drainage and sanitation are life-saving services. Do them properly, and you build a business that communities trust.

lessons.title: Module 8 Lesson 5: Running a Profitable Plumbing Business in Africa
lessons.body: Technical skill alone does not build a plumbing business. You need pricing, marketing, record-keeping, customer care, and a plan for growth. This lesson is about the business side of plumbing in Africa, where cash flow is tight, competition is real, and reputation is everything. Start with your legal and financial foundation. Register your business. In many countries, you can register a sole proprietorship or a limited company. Get a tax identification number. Open a business bank account. Keep business money separate from personal money. This discipline helps you see profit and loss clearly. If you are in a country with a VAT threshold, monitor it. If you employ people, comply with labour laws, pay wages on time, and contribute to social security if required. Insurance matters. Get public liability insurance if available. Get vehicle insurance. Get health insurance for your team if possible. In some countries, workers compensation is mandatory. Insurance protects you from a single accident wiping out your business. Pricing. Many plumbers underprice because they guess. Instead, calculate your costs. For each job, list materials, labour, transport, tools, and overhead. Add a profit margin of 20 to 30 percent. Add a contingency of 10 percent. For service calls, charge a call-out fee plus labour plus parts. For installations, quote a fixed price after a site visit. Never quote from a phone call alone. A site visit reveals access, pipe routes, wall types, and hidden problems. For maintenance contracts, charge a monthly or quarterly fee. That recurring revenue stabilises your cash flow. Payment terms. In Africa, late payment is common. Ask for a deposit of 50 percent for materials before starting. For large jobs, invoice in stages. For small jobs, collect payment on completion. Accept mobile money, bank transfer, and cash. Give a receipt every time. Use a simple invoice book or a phone app. Track who owes you. Follow up politely but firmly. Do not start the next phase until the previous invoice is paid. Marketing. Word of mouth is powerful, but it is not enough. Build a simple brand. Choose a business name, get a logo, and print business cards and stickers. Put your name and number on your vehicle and your toolbox. Create a WhatsApp Business profile with your services, photos, and location. Ask happy clients for reviews and referrals. Offer a small discount for referrals. Partner with real estate agents, hardware shops, and property managers. They meet clients every day. Give them a commission for referrals. Join local business associations. Attend community meetings. In rural areas, work with churches, mosques, and schools. Customer care. Answer your phone. Arrive on time. Wear clean clothes. Protect the client's floors and furniture. Clean up after work. Explain what you did and why. Give a warranty on your work, for example three months on labour. If something fails, fix it quickly. A complaint handled well creates a loyal client. A complaint ignored creates a bad reputation. Record-keeping. Keep a job book. For each job, record the date, client name, address, phone number, work done, materials used, labour hours, total charge, amount paid, and balance. Keep receipts for materials and transport. At the end of each month, add up income and expenses. Calculate your profit. If you are not making a profit, find out why. Maybe your prices are too low. Maybe you are buying materials retail and should buy wholesale. Maybe your transport costs are too high. Maybe you are doing too many small jobs and not enough large ones. Team building. You cannot grow alone. Hire apprentices and technicians. Train them. Pay them fairly. Give them responsibility. Send them for short courses. Create a simple system for job assignment, quality checks, and customer feedback. A team multiplies your capacity. But a team also multiplies your problems if you do not manage it. Set clear rules. Check work. Reward good performance. Tools and transport. Good tools save time and improve quality. Invest in a pipe cutter, a threading machine, a pressure test pump, a drain auger, a multimeter, and a leak detector. Buy a reliable vehicle or motorcycle. Keep it maintained. A breakdown on the way to a job costs money and reputation. Stock management. Keep common materials in stock: pipes, fittings, valves, cement, tape, and seals. But do not overstock, because cash tied up in stock is cash not available for wages. Use a simple stock card. Reorder when stock reaches a minimum level. Buy in bulk when you can get a discount, but only for items you use often. Growth strategy. Start with residential service and repair. Then move into installations. Then move into commercial and institutional contracts. Then move into specialised services like solar pumps, water treatment, and biogas. Each step requires new skills and new certifications. Invest in training. Read manuals. Watch videos. Attend workshops. Join professional associations. In many African countries, there are plumbing associations that offer certification and networking. Join them. They also help you lobby for better standards and fair competition. Ethics. Do not steal. Do not use substandard materials. Do not lie about what you did. Do not overcharge. Do not abandon a job. Your reputation is your most valuable asset. In a small town, news travels fast. In a city, online reviews travel fast. Be honest, and you will be recommended. Be dishonest, and you will be avoided. Financial planning. Save money for slow months. In many African countries, construction slows during the rainy season. Plan for that. Save for tools, vehicle repairs, and taxes. Keep a reserve of at least three months of operating costs. If you can, invest in a small piece of land or a rental property. That gives you security. Common mistakes. No records. No contracts. No deposits. No insurance. No marketing. No training. No savings. No separation between business and personal money. Underpricing. Overpromising. Hiring without training. Expanding too fast. In summary, plumbing is a noble trade and a real business. Master your craft, but also master your numbers. Serve your clients well. Train your team. Save your money. Grow step by step. That is how you build a plumbing business that lasts in Africa.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Water Quality Testing, Disinfection, and Safe Plumbing Practice for African Water Systems

This practical reference lesson supports Module 8 by giving plumbers, technicians, and small water-service businesses a single, field-ready guide to protecting the water that flows through the systems they install. In much of Africa, a plumbing job does not end when the pipe holds pressure â it ends when the water coming out of the tap is safe to drink. Customers increasingly ask for proof of water quality, and being able to test, treat, and document water safety is a direct route to higher-value contracts with schools, clinics, guesthouses, food processors, and NGOs. This lesson covers the core tests you can run on site, the disinfection methods that work under African conditions, and the business case for selling water-safety services as a recurring revenue line.

Water quality problems in African plumbing systems usually come from four places: contaminated source water, poorly sealed or uncleaned storage tanks, cross-connections and backflow during low pressure, and biofilm in pipes that sit idle. A plumber who understands these failure points can charge for assessment, treatment, and monitoring â not just pipe and fittings. The diagram above shows the chain you should inspect on every job. Each stage is a billable service point and a chance to prevent the next customer complaint.

Core Field Tests and What the Numbers Mean

You do not need a laboratory to catch most problems. A basic field kit â turbidity tube or meter, pH strips or meter, free chlorine test (DPD or color comparator), and a compact microbiology kit such as a portable incubation-based coliform test â costs roughly the same as a mid-range pipe wrench set and pays for itself on two or three jobs. The table below gives the key parameters, acceptable ranges, and the practical action to take when a reading is out of range.

Table 1: Field water quality parameters, target values, and corrective action
ParameterTarget / acceptable rangeWhy it mattersAction if out of range
Turbidity< 5 NTU (ideally < 1 NTU)Cloudy water shields pathogens from disinfection and signals contaminationInvestigate source; clean tank; pre-filter before chlorination
pH6.5 â 8.5Affects chlorine efficiency and pipe corrosionAdjust dosing; check source chemistry; avoid aggressive water on metal pipes
Free chlorine residual0.2 â 0.5 mg/L at point of use (WHO)Confirms disinfection and protects against recontaminationRe-chlorinate; check for chlorine demand from organics or ammonia
Thermotolerant coliforms / E. coli0 CFU per 100 mLDirect indicator of faecal contaminationStop drinking use; shock-chlorinate; re-test before release
Total dissolved solids (TDS)< 1000 mg/L (palatability)High TDS affects taste, scaling, and some treatment optionsConsider reverse osmosis or alternative source for drinking
Iron< 0.3 mg/L (aesthetic)Stains fixtures, encourages iron bacteria and biofilmAerate/filter; review borehole casing and pump materials

Sources for the ranges above: WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality, 4th edition (2017) and WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme guidance on drinking-water quality. For African field conditions, note that turbidity is often the first and cheapest indicator to act on â if you can only afford one meter, buy a turbidity meter and a free chlorine comparator.

Disinfection Methods Compared for African Conditions

Disinfection is where plumbing work becomes a health service. The choice of method depends on source quality, power availability, customer budget, and the customer's ability to keep the system running. The table below compares the main options with realistic cost and operating notes for African homes, schools, clinics, and small businesses.

Table 2: Disinfection and treatment options â suitability and operating notes
MethodBest forIndicative cost / inputOperating notes
Chlorination (liquid bleach / NaDCC tablets)Tanks, boreholes, piped supplies, emergency responseLow capital; recurring chemical costDose to achieve 0.2â0.5 mg/L free residual; test daily in busy systems
BoilingHouseholds with reliable fuelFuel cost; no equipmentBring to rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 2000 m altitude)
Ceramic / membrane filtrationHousehold and school point-of-useMedium capital; replacement cartridgesRequires cleaning regime; does not leave residual protection
UV point-of-useClinics, offices, guesthouses with stable powerHigher capital; electricityNeeds clear water (low turbidity) and lamp replacement schedule
Solar disinfection (SODIS)Emergency and rural household useVery low â PET bottles and sunlight6 hours in full sun; needs clear bottles and clear water
Solar / thermal pasteurisation systemsSmall institutions with spaceMedium capitalOutput depends on sunlight; combine with safe storage

Cost and method comparisons draw on WHO household water treatment and safe storage guidance and on the WHO/UNICEF JMP drinking-water reports. For African plumbers, the practical rule is: chlorinate storage and distribution, filter or boil at point of use where customers cannot manage chemicals, and always leave the customer with a simple test they can run themselves.

â  SAFETY WARNING â CHEMICALS AND CONTAMINATED WATER
  • Chlorine products are corrosive. Wear gloves and eye protection, work in a ventilated area, and never mix chlorine with acids or ammonia â toxic gas can be released.
  • Store chlorine and treatment chemicals away from children, food, and animal feed, in clearly labelled containers. Never decant into drink bottles.
  • Treat any water with confirmed E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms as unsafe for drinking, cooking, or brushing teeth until it has been disinfected and re-tested.
  • After shock-chlorinating a tank or borehole, flush the system and re-test before returning it to drinking service. Do not assume a smell of chlorine equals safe water.
  • If you suspect chemical contamination (pesticides, fuel, heavy metals) rather than microbial contamination, do not attempt to treat on site â refer the customer to a laboratory and alternative source.

Turning Water Safety into Recurring Business

Water safety is one of the few plumbing services that repeats. A customer who pays once for a tank clean and chlorination will pay again every three to six months. Schools, clinics, guesthouses, restaurants, and food processors often need documented water testing for funders, regulators, or certification. Position your business to offer three tiers: (1) a one-off water safety audit with written results; (2) a quarterly tank cleaning and disinfection service; and (3) an annual monitoring contract with test records and a simple report. In many African markets, the annual contract is the most profitable because it smooths cash flow and builds a referral base among institutions.

Price the service on value, not on chemical cost. A tank clean that prevents a clinic from closing due to contaminated water is worth far more than the bleach it consumes. Keep a simple record sheet for every site: date, source, test results, treatment applied, and next service date. That record becomes your marketing asset â it proves you are a professional water-safety provider, not just a pipe fitter.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Test source, storage, and point-of-use water separately â contamination often enters between stages.
  • Record turbidity, pH, free chlorine residual, and coliform result for every site visit.
  • Clean and disinfect storage tanks at least every 6 months, or quarterly for institutional clients.
  • Maintain 0.2â0.5 mg/L free chlorine residual at the tap where chlorination is used.
  • Never mix chlorine with acids or ammonia; wear gloves and eye protection when dosing.
  • After any repair, shock-chlorinate, flush, and re-test before returning the system to service.
  • Give the customer a simple written result and a next-service date â this is your contract renewal tool.
  • Refer suspected chemical contamination to a laboratory; do not attempt on-site treatment.

Further Reading

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a vent stack in a plumbing drainage system?
options: A) To increase water pressure at fixtures
B) To equalize air pressure and allow proper drainage
C) To filter waste before it enters the sewer
D) To heat water for the building
quiz.explanation: A vent stack equalizes air pressure in the drainage system so water can flow freely and sewer gases are safely released.

quiz.q: Which material is most commonly used for residential water supply lines due to its resistance to corrosion and ease of installation?
quiz.explanation: Copper is widely used for water supply lines because it resists corrosion and is easy to work with.

quiz.q: What does the term trap seal refer to in a plumbing fixture?
options: A) The water barrier that prevents sewer gas from entering a building
B) The rubber gasket around a toilet base
C) The valve that controls water flow to a faucet
D) The cap on a cleanout opening
quiz.explanation: A trap seal is the water held in a fixture trap that blocks sewer gases from entering the building.

quiz.q: When soldering copper pipe, what is the purpose of applying flux?
options: A) To cool the pipe during heating
B) To add color to the joint
C) To increase water flow inside the pipe
D) To clean the metal and help solder flow into the joint
quiz.explanation: Flux cleans the copper surface and promotes solder flow for a strong, leak-free joint.

quiz.q: What is the minimum recommended slope for a horizontal drain pipe of 2 inches diameter in most plumbing codes?
quiz.explanation: A 2 inch drain pipe typically requires a slope of 1/4 inch per foot to ensure proper drainage.

quiz.q: Which device is installed to prevent backflow of contaminated water into a potable water supply?
options: D) Check valve on a sump pump
quiz.explanation: A backflow prevention assembly stops contaminated water from reversing into the clean water supply.

quiz.q: What is the main function of a water hammer arrestor?
options: B) To filter sediment from water
C) To absorb pressure surges and reduce pipe noise
quiz.explanation: A water hammer arrestor absorbs sudden pressure changes that cause banging noises in pipes.

quiz.q: Which type of pipe is best suited for underground sewer lines because of its strength and resistance to chemicals?
quiz.explanation: PVC pipe is durable, chemical resistant, and commonly used for underground sewer lines.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a water storage tank in an African home or business?
options: A) To filter all contaminants from water
B) To store water for use during supply interruptions
C) To heat water for domestic use
D) To increase water pressure directly
quiz.explanation: Storage tanks provide a buffer so water is available when mains supply or pumping is interrupted, which is common in many African settings.

quiz.q: When sizing a water storage tank for a household, which factor is most important to determine first?
options: A) The colour of the tank
B) The daily water demand of the occupants
C) The brand of the tank
D) The distance from the tank to the road
quiz.explanation: Daily water demand, including peak usage, determines the required storage volume for reliability.

quiz.q: Which tank material is most suitable for above-ground potable water storage in hot African climates?
options: B) Food-grade polyethylene or lined steel
quiz.explanation: Food-grade polyethylene or properly lined steel resists corrosion and maintains water quality in high temperatures.

quiz.q: Why should a water storage tank be elevated or placed on a raised stand?
options: A) To make it easier to paint
B) To provide gravity pressure to outlets
C) To reduce the tank volume needed
D) To prevent water from freezing
quiz.explanation: Elevation creates gravity head, which can supply outlets without a pump or reduce pump load.

quiz.q: What is a key maintenance task for water storage tanks in dusty African environments?
options: A) Regularly clean and inspect the tank interior and vents
B) Add chlorine only once per year
C) Paint the inside with ordinary paint
quiz.explanation: Dust and debris can enter through vents, so periodic cleaning and inspection keep water safe.

quiz.q: Which pump type is commonly used for lifting water from a borehole in rural African areas?
quiz.explanation: Submersible pumps are placed inside the borehole and are efficient for deep water lifting.

quiz.q: What is the main factor when selecting a pump for an African water system?
options: A) The colour of the pump housing
B) Total head and required flow rate
C) The length of the power cable
D) The weight of the pump
quiz.explanation: Total head (lift plus friction losses) and flow rate determine whether a pump can meet demand.

quiz.q: Why is a pressure tank often installed with a pump in a water system?
options: B) To reduce pump cycling and maintain stable pressure
C) To increase the pump speed
quiz.explanation: A pressure tank stores pressurised water, reducing start-stop cycles and extending pump life.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of pump failure in African installations?
options: B) Sand and sediment entering the pump
quiz.explanation: Sand and sediment cause abrasion and blockages, leading to premature pump failure.

quiz.q: Which maintenance practice helps prevent pump overheating?
options: B) Ensuring adequate water flow around the motor for cooling
C) Closing the discharge valve fully
quiz.explanation: Submersible motors rely on water flow for cooling, so adequate flow prevents overheating.

quiz.q: Which pipe material is widely used for cold water distribution in African plumbing because it is cheap and easy to join?
quiz.explanation: uPVC is affordable, corrosion-resistant, and simple to joint with solvent cement, making it popular.

quiz.q: What is the correct method for jointing uPVC pipes?
options: B) Solvent cement after cleaning and priming
C) Threading and wrapping with tape
quiz.explanation: uPVC joints require cleaning, priming, and solvent cement for a strong, leak-free bond.

quiz.q: Why is pressure testing important after installing a plumbing system?
options: A) To check for leaks and verify joint strength
quiz.explanation: Pressure testing reveals leaks and weak joints before the system is put into service.

quiz.q: Which pipe material is most suitable for hot water lines in African homes?
quiz.explanation: PEX and copper withstand higher temperatures, unlike standard uPVC.

quiz.q: What is a common challenge for drainage systems in African cities?
options: B) Blockages from solid waste and inadequate maintenance
C) Excessive use of copper pipes
quiz.explanation: Solid waste and poor maintenance frequently block drains, causing overflows and health hazards.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a vent pipe in a drainage system?
options: A) To release sewer gases and equalise pressure
C) To increase water flow to taps
quiz.explanation: Vent pipes allow gases to escape and prevent trap siphonage by equalising pressure.

quiz.q: Which type of sanitation system is suitable for areas without a central sewer network in Africa?
options: B) Direct discharge to a river
C) Open pit latrine inside the house
quiz.explanation: Septic tanks with soakaways treat waste on-site where sewers are unavailable.

quiz.q: Why should inspection chambers be installed at intervals in a drainage line?
options: A) To allow access for cleaning and inspection
quiz.explanation: Inspection chambers provide access points for clearing blockages and checking flow.

quiz.q: What is a key step in starting a profitable plumbing business in Africa?
options: B) Accurate pricing that covers labour, materials, and overheads
quiz.explanation: Accurate pricing ensures the business remains profitable and sustainable.

quiz.q: Why is record keeping important for a plumbing business?
options: A) To track income, expenses, and customer jobs
quiz.explanation: Records help monitor profitability, manage cash flow, and make informed business decisions.

quiz.q: What is a good marketing strategy for a new plumbing business in an African community?
options: A) Rely only on word of mouth and never advertise
B) Build a reputation through quality work and local referrals
D) Ignore social media and local radio
quiz.explanation: Quality work and referrals build trust and attract repeat and new customers.

quiz.q: Which practice helps ensure safety on a plumbing job site in Africa?
options: A) Wearing appropriate personal protective equipment
B) Working without checking for underground cables
quiz.explanation: PPE and site checks reduce injuries and comply with basic safety standards.
